articles.title: Lindsay Clancy juror reveals new details about lone holdout who caused mistrial
articles.summary: A juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial provided new details Thursday about the lone holdout on the panel, including that he acted out the killings on a water bottle during deliberations.
articles.body: A juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial provided new details Thursday about the lone holdout on the panel, including that he acted out the killings on a water bottle during deliberations. Nick Dargie, 25, was one of the three men on the 12-person jury tasked with determining whether Clancy should be held criminally responsible for the 2023 strangulation deaths of her three young children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old. He told “Good Morning America” on Thursday about his frustrations with the holdout juror, who has yet to be publicly identified. “I think we felt defeated,” Dargie said about the case’s conclusion. “We spent seven weeks on this trial, almost two months of, you know, all of our lives dedicated to it.” He is among at least five jurors — and the first male — who have spoken out about the case and what happened inside the deliberation room at Plymouth Superior Court last week. After more than 38 hours, the jurors could not reach a unanimous decision, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial after they deadlocked three times. On Thursday, defense attorney Kevin Reddington filed a renewed motion to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility on each of the three charges, arguing that the prosecution did not prove, beyond a reasonable doubt, that Clancy was not in psychosis at the time of the killings. Dargie told “Good Morning America” that toward the end of deliberations, the holdout juror would not engage in discussions with others or provide evidence that supported his reasoning, instead choosing to scroll on his phone. Ultimately, Dargie said, he confronted the holdout juror after the man mimicked the killings, tying an exercise band entered into evidence around an empty water bottle and pulling it tight. Dargie said he is not sure why the man did that. “I was shocked. It didn’t make any sense to me,” Dargie said. “We’re not in here to play detective or it’s not a game of Clue. This is serious.” Throughout the trial, Clancy’s defense attorney argued that she was in a state of psychosis when she strangled the children with exercise bands and therefore was not aware of what she was doing. The prosecution, however, argued she was not actually experiencing postpartum psychosis and planned the killings ahead of time. Three women on the jury told NBC Boston that the 11 jurors agreed to find Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility. The holdout wanted to convict, they revealed, but admitted he expressed doubt in the prosecution’s case. “It was definitely frustrating, mainly frustrating when [the holdout juror] explicitly said, ‘You know, I don’t know if the prosecution or the defense proved their case,’” Dargie told “GMA.” Reddington in the motion also pointed to the fact that in this case, every juror except one — who did not apply the reasonable-doubt standard — came to that same conclusion. “No rational jury could find beyond a reasonable doubt that she had no mental disease or defect when the Commonwealth’s own proof established that she did,” the motion said, noting the 11-1 jury split. And at first, Dargie said, a number of jurors thought Clancy was guilty of the crimes, and at times the jury’s votes differed day to day. A female juror who spoke with CBS Boston anonymously said many people on the jury were initially “firm in their beliefs,” and that she was one of the people who, at first, agreed with the holdout and thought Clancy was guilty. She explained how there was so much “gray area” and doubt in the case, and that ultimately, she switched her tune because she thinks Clancy is mentally unwell and that she’d get better help in a state mental health facility than in prison. Dargie told “GMA” that “once we laid out all of the evidence and how we saw it, that really brought everyone kind of on the same page, except for this one juror.” The female juror chalked it up to one person being unable to let go of their convictions. When that one juror didn’t agree with the group, Dargie said, he asked him to show evidence that “helped to prove what he was saying, but he couldn’t.” That’s what led the jury foreperson to send a note to the judge about the holdout during deliberations, explaining that he wasn’t meeting the burden of reasonable doubt the prosecution must overcome. Dargie acknowledged that it’s fair for someone to have a differing opinion, but said this particular juror would not engage and could not “find something to support his view.” Now, prosecutors must decide whether they want to retry Clancy. The next hearing for the case is scheduled for Sept. 29. Dargie, who was serving in the military overseas, said he’s “haunted” by the case. Specifically, he said, the recording of the 911 call made by Clancy’s then-husband, Patrick Clancy, when he found the dead children that night is seared into his memory. The recording was played in court and was not released to the public. “I’ve never heard something like that, like a scream like that, come out of someone’s mouth,” Dargie said of the recording. “It’s horrifying.” The anonymous female juror told CBS Boston that she will “never be the same after that 911 call.” Dargie also rejected online conspiracy theories that Patrick Clancy was actually the one who carried out the killings, noting that if anyone had heard the 911 calls, they would change their mind. “I think if they tried the trial again the way they did, I think nine times out of 10, I think the jury would come back with not guilty by reason of insanity, no doubt,” Dargie said.

articles.title: University of Tennessee condemns flyers appearing to celebrate Charlie Kirk assassination
articles.summary: Flyers at the University of Tennessee advertise a campus gathering celebrating Charlie Kirk's assassination anniversary, but the university is condemning it.
articles.body: The University of Tennessee-Knoxville is condemning messages that celebrate political violence after mysterious "Kirkaversery" [sic] flyers advertised a gathering apparently marking one year since Charlie Kirk’s assassination, declaring, "WE WILL CELEBRATE THE FIRST NEW YEAR AK (AFTER KIRK)." The flyers, images of which circulated widely on social media and by Libs of TikTok, advertise an 8 p.m. Sept. 10 gathering on the HSS Lawn, an outdoor green space at UT Knoxville. But the university told Fox News Digital that it is not sponsoring an event related to Kirk’s assassination and that no organization has registered to use the location for such a gathering. "The university is not sponsoring any event related to Charlie Kirk’s assassination, and no organization has registered to use the HSS Lawn or any other reservable space for any such event," a university spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement Wednesday. "At this time, the university has not determined whether the flyers are connected to anyone affiliated with UT." PORTLAND TATTOO ARTIST ADVERTISES $50 ‘KIRKIVERSARY’ NECK TATTOOS ON ANNIVERSARY OF CHARLIE KIRK’S DEATH The spokesperson added, "The University of Tennessee strongly condemns any message or activity that celebrates or makes light of violence or the loss of human life. We remain committed to ensuring our campus is a place that values civility and where human dignity is respected." It is unclear who is behind the apparent event. Kirk, the 31-year-old founder of Turning Point USA, was assassinated Sept. 10, 2025, while speaking at Utah Valley University during his "American Comeback Tour." Other advertisements for similar events have appeared at various schools across the country, with students at Georgetown University allegedly planning a Kirk "lookalike contest" for the anniversary of the conservative activist’s assassination. The event drew thousands of upvotes on Fizz, an anonymous social media platform popular with Georgetown students, according to screenshots shared with Fox News Digital from the school’s Turning Point USA chapter. DEMOCRATIC STUDENT GROUP TO PROTEST CHARLIE KIRK MEMORIAL AT CAMPUS WHERE HE WAS KILLED INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES Similarly, an apparent Kirk look-alike contest is being advertised at the University of South Carolina for Thursday. articles.body: An effort by American power companies to reduce local air pollution in the 1970s ended up creating a much wider environmental crisis, turning a local health problem into a continent-wide acid rain emergency. By building huge smokestacks to send coal emissions away from nearby towns, power companies pushed sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides into high-altitude winds. Instead of removing the pollution, the strategy carried these harmful chemicals hundreds of miles downwind, bringing acidic rain to forests, lakes and communities far from the power plants. Data collected in a major government investigation by the United States Government Accountability Office (GAO), titled Air Quality: Information on Tall Smokestacks and Their Contribution to Interstate Transport of Air Pollution (GAO-11-473), shows how the rapid spread of these giant structures changed air chemistry across North America.The rise of the giant chimneysIn 1970, the United States had only two industrial smokestacks taller than 500 feet. By 1985, the number had risen to more than 180 as power companies worked to meet new ground-level air quality standards under the Clean Air Act. Instead of installing expensive scrubbers or other filtering systems at the source, electricity producers turned to a method known as dispersion. Tall stacks allowed coal-fired power plants to meet National Ambient Air Quality Standards around the plant by releasing their emissions far above ground level. According to historical research published by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) through its National Center for Environmental Publications (NEPIS), scientists soon realised that releasing pollution at greater heights changed how power plant emissions moved and reacted in the atmosphere. When released from shorter stacks, sulfur dioxide (SO₂) and nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) generally settled on nearby land or reacted close to the ground. When released from heights of 500 to 1,000 feet, however, the pollutants entered stronger and faster winds higher in the atmosphere.Exporting pollution across state linesOnce carried into the upper troposphere, the harmful gases could travel much farther and remain in the atmosphere for longer. Sunlight, moisture and oxygen transformed SO₂ and NOₓ into sulfuric and nitric acids. These acidic compounds travelled across large regions before falling as acid rain, snow and fog. In many cases, they damaged ecosystems in states that produced little of the original pollution. The GAO report found that tall smokestacks were heavily concentrated along major industrial areas. About one-third of all US stacks measuring more than 500 feet were built in just five states around the Ohio River Valley, a major centre for coal-fired power generation. Because of prevailing winds, emissions from power plants in Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania and West Virginia travelled east and north. The resulting acid rain lowered the pH of freshwater lakes in New York's Adirondack Mountains and New England. It also removed important nutrients from forest soils and killed red spruce trees at higher elevations. In Canada, pollution from American power plants travelled long distances and made thousands of lakes in Ontario and Quebec more acidic. The problem led to major diplomatic disputes between Washington and Ottawa during the 1980s.Congressional intervention and legacy controlsAs officials recognised that tall smokestacks were simply moving pollution from one state to another, Congress amended the Clean Air Act in 1977 to limit their use as a main way of meeting pollution rules. Section 123 of the Act introduced Good Engineering Practice (GEP) limits for stack heights. The rules discouraged utilities from building stacks taller than needed to prevent local aerodynamic downwash. Despite the changes, many older tall smokestacks continued operating for decades without modern pollution controls. The GAO found that even by the late 2000s, 56 percent of coal-fired boilers connected to tall stacks did not have flue gas desulfurisation scrubbers to remove sulfur dioxide. Another 63 percent lacked advanced controls for nitrogen oxides. Most of these uncontrolled units were built during the construction boom before 1980. To deal with the continued movement of pollution across state lines, federal regulators eventually moved from rules on stack height to strict limits on emissions. The Acid Rain Program, created under the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, pushed power companies to install pollution-control equipment or switch to coal with lower sulfur content. The programme eventually cut regional sulfur emissions by more than 80 percent, showing that effective pollution control requires capturing harmful emissions at the source rather than simply sending them higher into the atmosphere.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Britain brought back wild bison after 6,000 years; their grazing could reshape forests and create new habitats for other wildlife
articles.summary: UK News: Wild bison have not been seen in Britain for around 6,000 years. European bison are now roaming West Blean and Thornden Woods near Canterbury as part .
articles.body: Wild bison have not been seen in Britain for around 6,000 years. European bison are now roaming West Blean and Thornden Woods near Canterbury as part of an ambitious conservation project to restore natural woodland processes. As per BBC, it once roamed widely across the continent, from Scotland to Siberia, before disappearing from the wild in the early 20th Century.Bringing these animals back to Britain is more than restoring a species that has been gone for thousands of years. Their grazing and movement through the woodland can help restore ecological processes that have been missing from Britain for generations.How is the ‘Blean Bison Project’ bringing bison back to BritainThe return of European bison to Britain is being led by the Blean Bison Project in West Blean and Thornden Woods near Canterbury. Wildwood Trust and Kent Wildlife Trust launched the project in 2019 with the aim of restoring natural woodland processes. The idea is to allow bison and other conservation grazers to influence the landscape through their everyday behaviour. European bison are described as a keystone species and ecosystem engineer because their movements can alter habitats around them. The project seeks to create a healthier and more biodiverse woodland by allowing natural processes to play a greater role in shaping the environment.How do bison help create new habitats in the woodlandEuropean bison can transform their surroundings simply through the way they live. Their grazing and movements can change vegetation and create varied spaces within woodland. As bison move through the woodland, their size and behaviour can gradually change the landscape around them. They also rub against trees and strip bark, which produces dead wood that can provide habitats for woodpeckers, bats and fungi. These areas can become suitable for insects, wildflowers and sand lizards. Their activity can also open up the woodland canopy, which can allow more sunlight to reach the forest floor and create the conditions for dormant seeds to grow.How did the bison population grow in the Blean woodlandThe Blean herd began to take shape in 2022, when the first four adult bison arrived from wildlife parks in Scotland, Ireland and Germany. The matriarch reached the woodland from a wildlife park in Scotland in July, followed by two females from Fota Wildlife Park in Ireland. A bull then arrived from Sababurg Wildlife Park in December.The arrival of the adults was soon followed by the birth of a new generation. ‘Female Two’ gave birth to the first Blean calf in September 2022. In November 2023, the matriarch gave birth to another calf, marking another step in the herd’s growth. From the four adults that arrived in 2022, the herd has therefore grown through a series of successful births, establishing a breeding population in the woodland.Why is the return of bison important for Britain’s wildlifeWildwood Trust describes European bison as a keystone species whose behaviour can create complex habitats for other wildlife. Their activities include grazing, seed dispersal, trampling and nutrient cycling. The project also links this approach to wider concerns about declining biodiversity and the need for more natural woodland management. The Blean herd has already produced an important milestone. The male calf born in November 2023 was the first wild bison to be conceived and born in the UK for thousands of years, marking another stage in the species’ return.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Brics turns 25: How a Goldman Sachs acronym became a global power bloc
articles.summary: India News: The 18th Brics Summit is set to take place in New Delhi on September 12-13, bringing together leaders of the expanded grouping at a time when wars, tr.
articles.body: The 18th Brics Summit is set to take place in New Delhi on September 12-13, bringing together leaders of the expanded grouping at a time when wars, trade tensions and a shifting global order are testing its ability to act as a united bloc.India is hosting the summit as the current Brics chair, with the grouping now comprising 11 members and 10 partner countries.Under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” New Delhi has placed greater focus on cooperation across economic and financial issues, technology, energy, development and global governance.The scale of that transformation becomes clearer when traced back to the origins of Brics, a term coined 25 years ago by a Goldman Sachs economist to describe four emerging economies that he believed would become major drivers of global growth.From a Wall Street acronym to a global groupingTwenty-five years ago, Brics did not exist as a political grouping. It was a term coined by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O’Neill in 2001 to describe Brazil, Russia, India and China as emerging economies that could become major drivers of global growth.His paper, Building Better Global Economic BRICs, argued that the weight of these economies in the world economy would rise significantly and called for their greater representation in global policymaking forums.The transition from an economic concept to a government-led grouping began in 2006, when the foreign ministers of Brazil, Russia, India and China met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. The first summit of their leaders followed in 2009 in Yekaterinburg, Russia, giving the grouping a formal leaders-level platform.The following year, South Africa joined, turning BRIC into Brics and giving the grouping its first member from Africa.The next major transformation came at the 2023 Johannesburg Summit, when Brics agreed to its first large-scale expansion. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE were invited to join from January 1, 2024. Indonesia subsequently became the bloc's 11th full member in January 2025.The expansion also created a partner-country category, allowing a wider group of developing economies to engage with Brics without becoming full members.Why Brics matters in the changing global orderBrics has evolved from a forum focused largely on economic cooperation into a broader platform for emerging and developing economies seeking a greater role in global governance.Its members have repeatedly called for reforms in institutions such as the United Nations and international financial institutions, arguing that the architecture of global governance should better reflect the changing balance of economic power.Its growing importance is also backed by institutions created by the grouping itself. The New Development Bank, established in 2015, was designed to mobilise resources for infrastructure and sustainable-development projects in Brics and other emerging and developing economies.The bloc's significance has increased further with its expansion. The addition of countries such as Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the UAE and Indonesia has widened Brics' economic and geographic reach and strengthened its claim to be a platform for the Global South.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Houthis capture Yemeni town of Mocha: Why it’s important
articles.summary: The Houthi seizure of Mocha threatens global trade routes, severs vital supply lines, and displaces thousands in Yemen.
articles.body:
Houthi forces grabbed control of the Yemeni port city of Mocha on Thursday, in a major offensive that comes amid escalated fighting between the Iran-aligned movement and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government.

Hundreds of women and children left Mocha, seeking shelter in the Saudi-backed government-controlled provinces of Lahij and Aden, as the growing violence also threatened to exacerbate an already devastating humanitarian crisis across the Taiz and al-Hodeidah provinces, where more than 20,000 people have been displaced due to clashes over the past two weeks.

Al Jazeera’s Yemeni affairs editor, Ahmed al-Shalafi, highlighted the immediate civilian toll of the military shift. “Areas south of Hodeidah and Mocha witnessed waves of displacement towards Dhubab and Aden,” he said.

The fall of Mocha is the culmination of a massive Houthi offensive that exposed vulnerabilities within government-aligned defences. According to al-Shalafi, the Houthis applied pressure from three distinct axes starting on September 3: western Taiz, southern Hodeidah, and Mocha city itself.

The combat was intense on the outskirts of Mocha.

A key factor that helped the Houthis take control of the city was the withdrawal of the National Resistance Forces from the fighting, said al-Shalafi and Al Jazeera correspondent Maha Ali, who was reporting from Taiz.

The National Resistance, led by Tareq Saleh — nephew of Yemen’s former President Ali Abdullah Saleh, who was killed by the Houthis after initially allying with them — has been a central part of the Saudi-backed alliance, and the internationally recognised government it leads.

The Houthis took control of Mocha “following the withdrawal of the National Resistance Forces from them at dawn today and their movement towards Mocha”, al-Shalafi said. He added that it is unclear whether the National Resistance Forces withdrew “to arrange their ranks, or for a military reason, or due to their inability to withstand the intense military formations”.

According to Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, Saleh ordered forces to execute “a tactical withdrawal and repositioning in exchange for the Houthis’ advance in the al-Waziyah and Mawza fronts”, and instructed them to establish an alternative command centre.

The conflict is rapidly spilling over into maritime and distant terrestrial domains. Reuters quoted four unnamed sources as telling it that the Houthis “were launching attacks on the strategic Red Sea islands of Hanish”.

Simultaneously, Ali reported that “the military media of the National Resistance announced that the air aviation [of pro-government forces] targeted Houthi positions in Al-Tuhayta, Al-Salif, and Kamaran Island in Hodeidah governorate, while the Houthis launched two ballistic missiles towards the strategic Zuqar Island”.

Clashes also intensified inland. In Marib, “warplanes targeted Houthi reinforcements coming from Sanaa in Fardhat Nihm and others heading to north and south of Marib”, Ali reported.

Mocha’s geography makes its capture a global concern. The city sits approximately 75km (47 miles) north of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

Known as the Gate of Tears , this narrow passage is a critical artery for crude oil and fuel travelling from the Gulf to the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, as well as for Asian commodities and Russian oil.

Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry explained that controlling Mocha could give the Houthis a “stranglehold along the Bab al-Mandeb”.

Furthermore, it severs critical anti-Houthi supply lines, including “the road linking Mocha with Taiz” running south from Mocha, and supply lines through Mocha’s port.

“This is a turning point right now in the war,” defence policy analyst Wolfgang Pusztai told Al Jazeera. “This might lead to a breakdown of the government forces in the southern part of Yemen.”

“The port of Mocha was the last harbour fully under control of the internationally recognised government,” Pusztai said.

The international community is reacting with alarm.

A spokesperson for the United Kingdom’s Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office declared that “the Houthis bear full responsibility for this crisis”, and urged them to “cease their attacks and escalation immediately”.

Long before it became the focal point of a geopolitical crisis, Mocha was the Arabian Peninsula’s premier commercial hub and the birthplace of the global coffee trade. Mocha coffee gets its name from the city.

Mentioned in ancient Himyarite texts as “Makhn”, the city was first seized by Abyssinians in 517 AD before they were expelled by the Himyarite King Dhu Nuwas.

The Ottoman Empire overtook the city in 1536-1538 AD, transforming it into a military base to launch raids against the Portuguese.

Ironically, it was the Portuguese who became the first Europeans to taste Yemeni coffee when the Sheikh of Mocha hosted them and offered a “black drink that refreshes the body and relaxes the mind”.

According to historians, the Sufi scholar Ali bin Omar al-Shadhili first brought coffee to Mocha from Abyssinia.

The Ottomans initiated the first export operations through the port in 1536, sending beans via the Red Sea to Suez and Alexandria, where they were sold to Europeans. The Dutch secured their first commercial coffee deal in 1628, eventually smuggling live seeds to cultivate in Java and the Americas.

Mocha’s golden age extended through the 17th and 18th centuries. However, the city’s prominence faded in the late 19th century due to conflicts between the Ottomans and the British, and the rapid rise of rival ports in Aden and Hodeidah.

This economic decline devastated the local demographics: Mocha’s population plummeted from approximately 20,000 in the 19th century to just 1,000 in the 1930s, before a slow recovery brought the numbers back up to over 10,000 by 2004.

articles.title: US resumes immigrant visa processing for Hungary, Poland while wider pause continues: What it means
articles.summary: US News: The US has resumed immigrant visa processing for applicants in Hungary and Poland, even as immigrant visa processing remains disrupted at US embassies.
articles.body: The US has resumed immigrant visa processing for applicants in Hungary and Poland, even as immigrant visa processing remains disrupted at US embassies and consulates in much of the world.The selective restart comes after the Trump administration earlier halted immigrant visa processing on a much broader scale. The latest move has raised questions about why Hungary and Poland have been allowed to resume processing while applicants elsewhere remain in limbo.According to Reuters, the White House directed US missions in Hungary and Poland to prioritise immigrant visa processing. The US government has not publicly explained why the two countries were singled out.Why is there a worldwide pause on immigrant visa processing?The development is particularly significant because the US had initially announced a suspension affecting nationals of 75 countries in January 2026. The State Department said the policy was aimed at applicants it considered at high risk of becoming a “public charge” — meaning someone dependent on public benefits in the US.However, that January policy was later challenged in court. On August 21, a federal judge ruled against it, finding the policy unlawful. The State Department subsequently acknowledged that the January pause was no longer in effect.That did not mean immigrant visa interviews immediately returned to normal.Instead, the State Department introduced a new training programme for consular officers on how to assess whether applicants could financially support themselves in the US. The department then temporarily paused immigrant visa interviews globally while officers were trained under the new system.This is why the current situation is confusing: the original 75-country suspension has been struck down, but a separate operational pause has continued to affect immigrant visa interviews.What is an immigrant visa?The impact is significant because immigrant visas are used by people seeking to move permanently to the US, including spouses, parents and children of American citizens and other family-sponsored immigrants, as well as employment-based immigrants.Applicants from countries including India have reported that their appointments were cancelled or postponed.For Indian applicants, the Hungary-Poland development does not mean that immigrant visa processing has broadly resumed worldwide.The immediate significance is that Washington has demonstrated that the global pause is not absolute. Two countries have been given priority while applicants elsewhere continue to wait for normal interview scheduling.The State Department has not said when the wider processing disruption will end. The training requirements could keep some missions affected for months because officers must complete self-training and then receive certification.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Flamingo chicks hatch at Curraghs Wildlife Park
articles.summary: Three Chilean flamingo chicks have hatched in Ballaugh, with more to come...
articles.body:
Four Chilean flamingo chicks have hatched at Curraghs Wildlife Park in Ballaugh, with more still to hatch, in what the park says could be "another fantastic" breeding season.

The chicks are born grey and can take up to two years to develop the pink colouring flamingos are known for.

Flamingos get their colour from pigments in the shrimp and algae they eat, so newly-hatched chicks stay grey for weeks before slowly turning pink.

The Chilean flamingo is classed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List, with the wild population in gradual decline.

articles.title: London’s latest Fourth Plinth sculpture is a woman going places
articles.summary: New York artist Tschabalala Self has installed a monumental statue of a Black woman taking a powerful step forward in Trafalgar Square.
articles.body: A new sculpture has been unveiled in London’s Trafalgar Square, where it will stand for the next two years. “Lady in Blue,” by New York-based artist Tschabalala Self, is a bronze statue of an anonymous young Black woman wearing a form-fitting blue dress, matching heels and glass beaded jewelry. She’s strong and she’s going places. It is the 16th statue to be installed on the so-called Fourth Plinth, as part of an ongoing public art commission first launched by the Royal Society of Arts and today supported by the Mayor of London, Arts Council England and Bloomsbury Philanthropies. “Lady in Blue” stands out against the 19th-century historical landmarks that already occupy the square, namely Nelson’s Column and Landseer’s Lions. Instead of commemorating the past, Self wanted to represent the contemporary everywoman. “I wanted to direct everyone’s attention to the future,” the artist said during an interview at Pilar Corrias gallery ahead of the statue’s unveiling. “I don’t think there are enough monuments that are about our shared future to come.” It is also one of the rare statues in the UK depicting a Black woman. Out of around 1,500 statues in London, just a handful represent women of color. Self, who is known for her distinct depictions of the Black female body that generate discourse around intersections of race, gender and sexuality, is not surprised by this statistic. “I really want people to take away from the sculpture the feeling that they can feel free to exist as they are without explanation,” she said. But, she adds, representation should not be the sole purpose of her sculptures. “It’s not that speaking about blackness minimizes the work, because I don’t believe that to be the case. It’s just that I don’t think that’s the focal point of the project,” Self said. “I also feel like when people enter the work through that framework, they’re already starting a process of reduction because they have come to name and define the figures by their identity politics.” This is Self’s first public sculpture in the UK since 2023, when her sculpture “Seated” was defaced after being installed in the English town Bexhill-On-Sea. Vandals spray painted the skin of the sculpted Black woman white. “I was very upset when the sculpture was vandalised, but ultimately that experience turned out being one that was very edifying for me,” Self said. “It highlighted how real people, not just figurative sculptures, experience these same kind of aggressions and acts of violence and intimidation in real life. So I feel like for those reasons, the sculpture did its work.” A community clean-up day was organised following the incident and the white paint was removed. “Through the restoration of the sculpture, it also showed people’s willingness and desire to overcome the societal ills.” With “Lady in Blue,” she feels prepared for more conversations about the importance of figuration and representing all identities in public art, “even if the conversations take a dark turn, because I know ultimately, it would be for the greater education of all parties involved,” she said. “Lady in Blue” is a striking addition to the London landmark with her jewelry, braided hair and matching lapis lazuli outfit —a shade which was inspired by the rare rock used as a pigment since antiquity. But more important is the statue’s powerful stride: “She’s not static,” Self said. “She has a desire to move, and in her having this courage to be optimistic and move forward, I hope that is going to be inspiring to all people who encounter her to know that this is something that’s also available to them — the ability to stride and to move forward,” she continued. With thousands of people walking through Trafalgar Square everyday, in one of the most diverse cities in the world, Self wants the public to see themselves reflected back in “Lady in Blue.” “I want her just to become a Londoner at the end of the day,” she said.

articles.title: Cause of Dunwich Heath wildfire cannot be determined
articles.summary: The fire and rescue service says any evidence that could point to the cause has been destroyed.
articles.body:
The cause of a huge wildfire that destroyed parts of a nature reserve could not be determined, according to a fire service.

Large parts of Dunwich Heath and of the neighbouring RSPB Minsmere on the Suffolk coast were destroyed by a fire the size of 210 football pitches, which started on 29 July.

It took Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service two weeks to stand down from the scene and while investigations have identified where the fire originated, its cause remained undetermined.

A spokesperson for the fire service said the severity of the blaze had meant any potential evidence on its cause had been destroyed.

"Following a detailed investigation into the Dunwich Heath wildfire, Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service has concluded that the cause of the fire cannot be determined," it said.

"While investigators were able to identify the general area where the fire originated, the severity of the fire meant that any potential evidence that may have identified a cause was destroyed."

It added: "Although the cause remains undetermined, this incident serves as a reminder of how quickly fire can spread during periods of prolonged dry weather.

"We continue to encourage residents and visitors to take extra care in the countryside and follow wildfire prevention advice to help protect Suffolk's communities, wildlife and landscapes."

Tristan Gale, Suffolk County Council's cabinet member for the fire service, thanked those who had been involved in the response to the incident.

"While it is disappointing that the exact cause cannot be conclusively established, the incident reinforces an important message for all of us," he said.

"As periods of hot, dry weather become more common, we must all remain vigilant and do what we can to stop the risk of wildfire."

At its peak, 120 firefighters were at the scene, with all 35 of Suffolk's stations involved and many other crews called in from other counties.

The fire caused nearby holiday parks to be evacuated and volunteers stepped in to house those who had been displaced.

Local farmers also helped to create firebreaks to slow the spread and ultimately no properties were lost.

There had also been some positive signs of nature returning to the area.

articles.title: Why being ‘fortunate’ is more than just a T-shirt slogan for former WWE star Mosh
articles.summary: The Headbangers' Mosh reveals how his WWE tag team wrestling career and thyroid cancer survival inspired the Live Fortunate lifestyle brand.
articles.body: Any pro wrestling fan who tuned into "Monday Night Raw" during the peak of the war between WWE (then the WWF) and World Championship Wrestling would likely see The Headbangers wreaking havoc on the tag team division. Mosh and Thrasher were, surprisingly, only one-time tag team champions during their careers with the company. Since leaving WWE, Mosh has transformed into an entrepreneur outside the ring and created a premium lifestyle brand that not only reflects his wrestling career but his life as a whole. COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK If you tell Chaz Warrington (Mosh) that he’s "lucky" to have been given the opportunities he’s had in his life, he will stop you in your tracks. He’s not "lucky," he’s "fortunate." The Live Fortunate brand he created carries a significance that goes beyond just a simple T-shirt slogan. It’s a mantra and a way of life he’s cultivated throughout his life. "So, Live Fortunate is based around if you've ever worked hard for something in your life and someone's told you you're lucky, this brand's for you," he told OutKick Dropkick in a recent interview. "I'm very fortunate in my life with my past with wrestling, and I work a lot with nonprofits here in South Florida and because I have my wrestling background and because of the nonprofits I work with, a lot of opportunities have popped up for me as far as going to black-tie events and being able to make an impact on the community. "And then with wrestling, different interviews come up. I'm fortunate enough to where WWE calls me and I can go up to their Performance Center in Orlando (Florida) and work with the NXT kids. So, I look at all of that as things that I've worked for, that have become opportunities because I've worked hard and I've done the work. I've put the time in. I've done the grind of working early in the morning. With my sales job that I have, I cold-called in 100-degree weather in a suit, walking up and down the street, which all of that has cultivated into different opportunities I've been given and I've earned." Warrington said he thought of it while at his camp. When one member of his group told him he was "lucky," he immediately said "luck has nothing to do with it," despite the T-shirt he was wearing at the time was a Lucky Brand clothing item. He told the person he would be wearing a different T-shirt when he saw them next. He said he was creating the T-shirt when he realized that being fortunate meant more to him than just a word on some cloth. "The more I started getting into it and I thought about it, I'm like, this isn't just a T-shirt. It signifies something," he recalled. "For instance, I have another shirt that has a rhinoceros on it and it says ‘Live Fortunate’ on it. And then there's all the different words of gratitude, opportunities, and earning things — it's all like within there. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "So, that's kind of the message behind the brand. If you've worked hard for anything and someone's told you you're lucky, you're not ‘really lucky,’ you're fortunate because you've earned that opportunity. It's a clothing line. More of a premium lifestyle brand that I'm looking at. It's basically the message of getting that across. That's kind of what the basis is behind it." Warrington said he has been fortunate to be able to give back to his community as well through the Junior Achievement of South Florida, teaching kids about financial literacy and sharing his life experiences with the younger generation. There’s another reason for Warrington to feel fortunate, too. He’s a cancer survivor. Warrington was diagnosed with thyroid cancer in 2017. He told OutKick Dropkick that he wasn’t one to worry about something unless there was something to worry about and keeping that even-keeled mindset helped push any negative thoughts out of his head to stay focused on the task at hand. "I think that mindset for me kind of helped. That with the fact that I was like, I'm young. I have a family I still need to take care of. I need to be here, and I just look at things from a positive side. I always try to find a silver lining in something. I don't look at something as my glass is half empty or half full – it’s always three-quarters full, and I can always fill it back up. So, I think that that's the part that really helped me pull through that. "And it's funny because there's a lot of times I don't think of myself as a survivor. I am, but I don't really look at it that way because, for me, what I went through in my mind was relatively easy. Again, there was a problem, there was a fix, we moved on. There are so many other people out there, their cancer was a lot worse or who are going through a lot worse things than me. So, if I could get the opportunity to talk to them about just trying to stay in a positive mindset, to find the silver lining – the glass is always three-quarters full and you still have an opportunity to refill it. I think that's kind of what got me through that and the message that, when I do talk to people, I try to get across." Warrington said he learned the mind truly is a powerful thing and may be something that doesn’t get enough credit. articles.title: At least 20 killed in school fire in rebel-held DR Congo city
articles.summary: Victims from the fire in AFC/M23-held Bukavu include primary school students, say officials and media reports.
articles.body:
A fire in Democratic Republic of the Congo’s (DRC) rebel-controlled city of Bukavu has killed at least 20 people, including students, according to local media and medical sources.

United Nations Radio Okapi, quoting local authorities, said 20 people were killed and an unspecified number injured on Thursday when a fire broke out in the Chimpunda district of Bukavu, South Kivu’s provincial capital.

The report said the incident took place at Ujamaa and Furaha primary schools and a nearby settlement at about 8am local time.

The fire was “followed by a violent stampede that forced students to trample over one another or look for a dangerous way out; many of them fainted and others lost consciousness”, local leader Patrice Buduge told the AFP news agency.

Dunia Masumbuko Bwenge, an official from the rebel administration, told the Reuters news agency 24 people had died – 19 ‌girls and five boys.

Bwenge, who is vice governor of South Kivu province in the government appointed by the Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 movement, added that 29 others were injured.

Christophe Zigashane, a nurse at a local clinic, told AFP at least 14 children were among those killed.

“We received around 50 students, including several teachers, in a critical state of asphyxia,” he said. “Among them, 10 were dead and four others died at the scene. That makes a total of 14 deaths, all under 10 years old.”

Footage verified by Al Jazeera showed the blaze consuming a number of houses, amid a spread of flames that reached the two schools.

Local media said the blaze also ravaged between 300 and 500 homes and a clinic.

It added that the death toll remained provisional, and the cause of the fire was yet to be established.

Several people were treated for smoke inhalation, with some said to be in critical condition.

Congolese media noted that Bukavu has experienced several fires in recent days, including a blaze that broke out last Sunday and destroyed more than 45 houses.

Bukavu has been controlled by AFC/M23 rebels since the group ⁠staged a lightning offensive in eastern DRC last ⁠year.

articles.title: Algeria to sever diplomatic ties with UAE after years of tension
articles.summary: The Algerian foreign ministry did not give a reason for the move but said it had exhausted all means.
articles.body:
Algeria is severing diplomatic ties with the United Arab Emirates after "provocative or hostile" acts by the Gulf state, its foreign ministry said.

"Algeria spared no effort to draw the Emirati side and warned it of the dire consequences that could result from its regrettable and unjustified behaviour," it said.

The statement did not provide any details on why Algeria has taken this step, but relations between the two countries have soured in recent years amid a series of regional disputes.

There has been no direct response from the UAE, but the president's diplomatic advisor said ties are not based on "riddles and signals that require decoding".

"Diplomatic relations are managed through rationality, communication and clarity of interests", Anwar Gargash wrote on X.

While he did not single out Algeria in his post, he said successful diplomacy was built on understanding and management of interests and differences.

"Ambiguity is not a policy, and noise does not compensate for the absence of vision," Gargash added.

The Algerian foreign ministry's statement - shared by state media - claimed that the UAE's behaviour had reached a point where it could no longer be tolerated, and that it had "exhausted all means of preserving bilateral relations".

The UAE ambassador was summoned to the ministry, where he was informed of the decision and told he had 48 hours to comply, it added.

The two countries' relations have increasingly become strained over recent years due to their opposing positions on several regional issues.

Algeria rejects the normalisation of diplomatic relations with Israel, which the UAE and Morocco - Algeria's neighbour and rival - have established ties with under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.

The UAE also supports Morocco's claim over Western Sahara in a decades-long dispute over its sovereignty, while Algeria has given its backing to the Polisario Front, an armed group which seeks an independent state there for the Sahrawi people.

articles.title: He was rejected as “too old” at 42; the former Special Forces soldier later became an entrepreneur and acquired an $8 million company

articles.body: After leaving a 22-year Army career that included Special Forces service, Jary Jackson expected his military experience to help him transition into civilian work. Instead, a veteran recruiter told him he was “too old at 42” and “unproven”. The rejection pushed Jackson towards entrepreneurship through acquisition. He eventually bought an $8 million company with just $35,000 of his own money. What began as a frustrating career setback became a turning point, leading the former soldier into business ownership and a new professional chapter.Jackson spent 22 years in the US ArmyJackson began his military career in Army infantry before leaving after four years and becoming a firefighter. After the September 11 attacks, he returned to the Army and eventually passed Special Forces selection. He went on to spend 22 years in the service, developing leadership and operational experience that would later shape his approach to business. The MILCOM Founders Podcast in ‘From Special Forces to Independent Sponsor with Jary Jackson’, hosted by Rod Loges describes how Jackson carried those lessons into civilian life, particularly the importance of identifying capable people and building teams around their strengths. His military background, however, did not immediately translate into the opportunities he expected after retirement.A recruiter told him he was “too old” at 42Jackson faced a difficult transition after leaving the Army. Despite his extensive military experience, he faced repeated rejection when applying for civilian roles. The rejection that stayed with him came from a veteran recruiter who told him he was “too old at 42” and “unproven”. Rather than accepting that assessment, Jackson began exploring other ways to use his experience. His story focuses on his move from military service into entrepreneurship and business acquisition.He discovered a way to buy a company rather than start oneJackson eventually discovered the search-fund and entrepreneurship-through-acquisition model, which gave him another route into business ownership. Instead of building a company from scratch, he could identify an established business and acquire it, using its existing operations as a foundation for growth. Jackson ultimately acquired an $8 million company with just $35,000 out of pocket. The experience helped turn his military background into an entrepreneurial advantage, particularly his ability to assess people, make decisions under pressure and focus on mission-oriented execution.His rejection became the foundation for a new business careerJackson later founded Intrepid Prosperity, a talent-management and human-capital company focused on connecting high-performing veterans and elite operators with organisations that need their skills. He also became CEO of TCS and founded Thurion Capital, an independent sponsor focused on acquiring and scaling lower-middle-market companies in areas including logistics, sustainment and technical services. The podcast describes Jackson’s central business philosophy as recognising that talent drives outcomes and that resumes alone do not reveal whether someone can succeed. The lesson behind his journey is therefore straightforward: being rejected at 42 did not end his career, it pushed him towards ownership.His company now focuses on defence and government contractingJackson has since turned his acquisition experience towards a broader investment strategy through Thurion Capital, an independent sponsor focused on acquiring and scaling businesses serving government and commercial customers, particularly in defence and other dual-use sectors. Public descriptions say the firm looks for companies with established operations that can be expanded rather than building businesses from scratch. As of 2026, Jackson is continuing to build Thurion Capital while pursuing acquisitions in the lower-middle market. articles.title: DHS proposes scrapping 60-day grace period for foreign workers after job loss
articles.summary: US News: The US department of homeland security (DHS) on Thursday released a draft proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period, currently available to certai.
articles.body: The US department of homeland security (DHS) on Thursday released a draft proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period, currently available to certain non-immigrant workers (such as H-1B and L-1 visa holders) following termination of employment. While the proposal covers several employment-based non-immigrant visa categories, from the perspective of the Indian diaspora, the most significant impact would be on H-1B visa holders, L-1 visa holders (those on intra-company transfers) and O-1 visa holders (this visa is given to those who are recognised for extraordinary ability).Under the existing framework, following a layoff or other termination of employment, these visa holders are typically granted a discretionary grace period of up to 60-days, or until the end of their authorised stay, whichever comes first. The grace period can provide valuable time to find another employer, seek a change of status (say transition to a B-visitor visa) or make arrangements to leave the US.The proposal marks a significant reversal of a policy DHS itself introduced in 2016. At the time, the agency recognised that the abrupt loss of employment was not necessarily the worker's fault and that allowing highly skilled workers time to find new employment could benefit both foreign workers and US employers.The proposed rule now argues that the 60-day provision goes against the employment-linked nature of these immigration classifications. DHS states: “The up to 60-day discretionary grace period disconnects the alien’s lawful status from the very basis of eligibility under these employment-based non-immigrant classifications.” The agency also says the earlier rule “did not sufficiently consider the negative impacts of the grace period provision.”Notably, DHS acknowledges that scrapping the grace period would carry human and economic costs. The department says some affected workers could suffer monetarily because they would have to leave the US and subsequently seek readmission rather than remain in the country while looking for new employment. It also acknowledges that some workers could receive Notices to Appear (NTAs) and potentially enter removal proceedings.DHS further recognises the extent to which foreign workers and their families may have put down roots in the US. In the proposal, it notes that such workers and their dependents may have “purchased houses, paid taxes, and may have otherwise invested in the local community in reliance on the alien’s continued stay in the US.” They may also have made career and personal plans on the assumption that they could remain in legal status for up to 60 days after their employment ended while seeking a new status.Despite such acknowledgement DHS concludes that the costs of retaining the grace period are outweighed by what it describes as the need to restore the employment-linked nature of the non-immigrant classifications and reduce the administrative burden on US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).The proposed rule is open for public comments and the entire process up to issue of a final rule could take several months.Cyrus D. Mehta, a US immigration attorney, states “If the discretionary 60-day grace period is eliminated, foreign nationals whose employment ceases prematurely (and their dependents) would no longer be maintaining status and would generally be required to depart the US immediately, unless USCIS exercises its separate discretion to forgive the lapse in status and allow the foreign national to change status or change employers within the country.”The potential impact on Indians is significant. According to the latest USCIS data for fiscal year ended Sept 30, 2025, 57,747 India-born beneficiaries accounted for 50.3 percent of the 1,14,806 H-1B petitions approved for initial employment. The concentration was substantially higher among continuing employment cases: 2,26,359 India-born beneficiaries accounted for 77.6 percent of the 2,91,542 H-1B petitions approved for continuing employment.Immigration attorneys point out that the Trump administration had already begun tightening the net around laid-off foreign workers in recent months. Workers using the 60-day period to seek a change to B-1/B-2 visitor status allowing them to remain lawfully in the US while looking for new employment, have increasingly faced Requests for Evidence (RFEs) and, in some cases, Notices of Intent to Deny (NOIDs).Thus, while currently the 60-day grace period currently remains until a final rule is introduced, transiting to a new visa status remains challenging.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Simon Le Bon delighted with Duran Duran stamp collection
articles.summary: The collection charts the band's rise from the Birmingham club scene to international stardom.
articles.body:
Simon Le Bon has said the new Royal Mail stamp collection featuring Duran Duran is a "massive visual validation of the band and its history".

The stamps are being released to celebrate the award-winning group's almost 48-year career and feature album artwork that charts their rise from the Birmingham club scene.

Le Bon said the stamp collection was a "pinch yourself" moment and added: "Having stamps is a bit far out. Nobody would have anticipated this at any time."

The band is famed for hits such as Rio, Hungry Like The Wolf and Ordinary World and achieved two UK number one singles and one chart-topping album.

The collection also includes a miniature sheet featuring their tour posters from the 1980s until the 2020s.

Le Bon said: "For so many years, we were struggling against the negativity. We're not a flash in the pan, and the stamps really vindicate us."

The 67-year-old also said: "When you see those album covers all lined up, all eight of them, you look at it [and] say, 'we've done a lot of work'.

"And we've done it together – we've stayed together – and it reminds us of that. I just feel so happy and fortunate to be part of all that."

The singer joined the group in 1980 alongside keyboardist Nick Rhodes, bassist John Taylor and drummer Roger Taylor.

Founder John described the collaboration as "a Duran Duran legacy project", while Roger said it made the band feel like "part of the cultural furniture".

"The band is almost set in stone now. Once you start getting things like this, there's an immortality," Roger added.

Royal Mail is selling a range of Duran Duran products along with the stamp release and said they were "celebrating Duran Duran's many firsts and achievements in music and technology".

articles.title: WWE broadcaster Corey Graves hypes Triplemania 34 before Night 1 in Las Vegas
articles.summary: Triplemania 34 brings Lucha Libre AAA to the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas on Friday, featuring Rey Mysterio vs. Omos and key WWE crossovers.
articles.body: September is a historic month in the world of Lucha Libre. Triplemania 34, the premier event for Lucha Libre AAA Worldwide and better known as AAA, will take place in the United States for the first time. Night 1 will be held at the MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas on Friday and will showcase some of the best pro wrestling the sport has to offer. Night 2 will take place at Arena CDMX in Mexico City on Sunday. The spectacle will showcase the talents who regularly perform on AAA programming on Saturday nights with a handful of familiar WWE stars mixed in. COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK For pro wrestling fans who may not have tuned into AAA in the past or have and are unsure about what Triplemania is all about, commentator Corey Graves broke it down in a recent interview with OutKick Dropkick. He compared the style and colorful nature of Lucha Libre to that of the Savannah Bananas. "So, I think most people would be familiar with WrestleMania. Most people, if you're not a pro wrestling fan, you're familiar with that brand. It's been massive for over 40 years. This is about to be the 34th installation of Triplemania, and Lucha Libre in Mexico is yes professional wrestling as we know it in America or around the globe, but it's very different. It's a unique cultural touchstone," he said. "There are bright colors and incredible action, and there's a lot of stuff that you will see on Raw or SmackDown including superstars who are heavily influenced by the Lucha Libre style. It's not exactly like you see on WWE, but it's the same. "And I've used the analogy quite a few times lately because I'm a big baseball fan. If you're a Major League Baseball fan, WWE is Major League Baseball. AAA, to me, is sort of, and I mean this in the best way possible, like the Savannah Bananas. It's still baseball. All of the things that you know and love about baseball still take place. It's just through a very different lens. It's about these insane characters and costumes and pageantry and the action. You have a lot of people who can't sit through a nine-inning major league game who will spend their last dollar on tickets to go see the Savannah Bananas because it's an event. It's a happening. That's kind of how Lucha has always been in Mexico. And now this is an opportunity to bring that to an American audience in Las Vegas. And a lot of people, Savannah Bananas aren't for them, but they still like baseball. You get both. It's kind of the closest way I can explain it without betraying everything." Graves said fans want to be a part of the action even though they may not fully understand the long history of Lucha Libre in Mexico. Essentially, it’s all about being there. "There’s incredible things. It's about moments. It's about memories," he said. "It's less about statistics and long-term records, etc. But it's about being there and just enjoying what's happening. And that's what AAA has become over the last year to me. You just want to be part of it even if you don't fully understand it. "And I wouldn't expect a lot of our audience to — that's sort of my job, to sort of bring everybody along and explain to them why these characters are important and what they mean and why it is different, and it's important to me to maintain some difference. You don't want to lose that flavor. You don't want to lose the essence of Lucha Libre. We can clean up the production. We can sprinkle in a few WWE superstars here and there. But at its core, it's still Lucha Libre and TripleMania is AAA's WrestleMania." It’s been a busy 18 months for WWE and Las Vegas. WWE held WrestleMania 41 and 42 at Allegiant Stadium in 2025 and 2026 respectively. Now, they’re bringing in high-octane action back to the city with one of the biggest events on the wrestling calendar. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Originally, the event was set to take place at the Luxor. But WWE and AAA were forced to move venues because of the interest in the event. "This is just me speaking off the top of my head. I can't say this with any sort of authority, but I would assume it shows the higher-ups, the people who make these decisions as to where to book the shows, when to book them, what to pour our resources into, specifically the fact that we were originally booked to be at the Luxor Hotel, and within days we were forced to move to the MGM Grand Garden Arena for capacity purposes because there was such a demand," Graves told OutKick Dropkick. "Now, obviously, there's a heavy Latino population around Las Vegas but hopefully it's showing that English-speaking audiences as well are learning or curious about this new product. It's available for free every Saturday night on YouTube if you're in the United States or around most of the globe, obviously, we have television in Mexico and into Central and South America, but no matter where you are, Saturday nights 10 o’clock, you can tune into this and see what it's about. And it's such a visual product. And I say that almost discrediting myself because my job is to explain why it's important, but you can put it on mute and you can just watch and be captivated by the masks and the costumes and there's so much pageantry in Lucha. It's really, not that there isn't in WWE, it's just different. It's a completely different animal." Night 1’s card features a bout between Rey Mysterio – the AAA general manager – and Omos. If Omos wins the match, he will be welcomed back to AAA. But if he loses, he will be forever shunned. Dominik Mysterio is set to be in Omos’ corner, while El Grande Americano will be behind Rey Mysterio. Dominik Mysterio and El Grande Americano are pulling double duty to a point. articles.title: Kore Bommeli enters no contest plea for manslaughter in Talina Galloway case | Dateline
articles.summary: Talina Galloway vanished from Wagoner, Oklahoma, in spring 2020. Her remains were discovered in Arkansas in January 2021. Her roommate, Kore Bommeli, was charged with murder, but has pleaded no contest to a lesser charge of manslaughter.
articles.body: It’s been more than five years since Kore Bommeli was arrested and charged with killing her roommate, Talina Galloway. Talina went missing in Wagoner, Oklahoma, in spring 2020. Dateline featured her story in May 2020 in its “Missing in America” series. In January 2021, following the discovery of Talina’s remains in Polk County, Arkansas, Bommeli was arrested and charged with first-degree murder and desecration of a human corpse. The trial was set to begin in an Oklahoma courtroom this week. Instead, last Friday, Bommeli accepted a last-minute plea deal, pleading no contest to a lesser charge of manslaughter, and to desecration of a human corpse, and possession of a firearm after a former felony conviction . Bommeli’s legal co-counsel, Bryan Cannonie, spoke to NBC affiliate KJRH after the plea was entered. “Kore is steadfast in her claim that she did not do this,” he said. “I think we even told the DA, we did not believe that Miss Bommeli would enter any plea to the case. We thought we were going to trial.” KJRH also spoke with District Attorney Jack Thorp. “We provided them with a plea offer after we had checked with the family to make sure that that’s something that they were good with, they were,” Thorp said. “I think that they wanted to see this case finally come to a conclusion.” Bommeli is already serving 35 years in Wisconsin for attempted murder in a separate incident. In Oklahoma, Bommeli was sentenced to 28 years, with credit for time served since 2021, on the manslaughter charge to be served concurrently with her Wisconsin sentence. She was also sentenced to five years on the weapons charge, to be served concurrently, and seven years for desecration of a human corpse, to be served consecutively to the Wisconsin sentence. “Our hopes are that she spends all her time in custody behind bars, and she thinks about the harm, the pain that she caused,” the district attorney told KJRH. articles.title: How a podcast community helped restore the controversial 'Gator Bait' chant for Florida football team
articles.summary: James Di Virgilio and his "Gator Nation Football Podcast" rallied fans to write to Dr. Stuart Bell, helping revive the banned "Gator Bait" chant.
articles.body: For anyone who went through it, 2020 felt like living in a parallel universe. The year was dominated by the Covid craziness that swept through the world as well as the myriad "cancellings" that took place, and college football in particular felt the effects of both. Games and traditions alike were severely altered or outright shut down as a result of the pandemic and its accompanying lunacy, and the Florida Gators' football program especially felt the brunt of this. COLLEGE FOOTBALL'S FIRST FULL SATURDAY IS HERE AND IT'S A CELEBRATION OF AMERICA AT ITS BEST Sure, the Gators still played a ten game, All SEC slate, but access to Ben Hill Griffin Stadium was greatly limited, as the stadium which normally seats upwards of 90,000 fans on gameday had its attendance whittled down to less than 20,000. In the wake of all of this, a tradition known affectionately around campus and throughout the community as "Gator Bait" was given the axe. School officials cited "racial undertones" as the reason for removing the chant, linking back to late 19th and early 20th century depictions of using African-American children as bait for alligators. The chant, at least in the context of the Florida football team, has much more innocent origins, being popularized in the 1990s by defensive back Lawrence Wright. THESE ONCE-ANNUAL COLLEGE RIVALRIES USED TO DEFINE COLLEGE FOOTBALL AND NEED TO MAKE A COMEBACK ASAP No one is more familiar with "Gator Bait" than James Di Virgilio, the popular podcast host of the "Gator Nation Football Podcast." Di Virgilio and his co-host, Allen Williams, started the podcast back in 2014 as a break from the monotony and blind homerism that is abundant in the local sports talk radio shows around Gainesville, where the two reside. Both are Florida graduates, and when they heard the news that "Gator Bait" was being shelved, Di Virgilio was perplexed. "I think, like any Gator fan, it was surprising at first," said Di Virgilio. "As far as anyone could tell, no one who had ever used the chant at Florida... had any idea there could be any connection to anything other than a gator eating our opponents, so to speak, in a humorous way." The GNFP host mentions other schools like LSU saying "Tiger Bait" as a rallying cry while receiving little to no backlash. "I think it was a chant that many Gators (fans), especially those who are maybe 90s or 2000s Gators, have fond memories of chanting at opponents when you're winning national championships, etcetera, therefore it conjured up those memories of yesteryear," he opined. COLLEGE FOOTBALL IS FINALLY BACK AFTER MONTHS OF NCAA LAWSUITS, NIL DRAMA AND CONGRESSIONAL FIGHTS Despite the seemingly innocuous nature of the cheer, "Gator Bait" was officially banned in 2020 out of what Di Virgilio deemed "an abundance of caution" during a time of heightened scrutiny. Meanwhile, in those years since the banning, the GNFP audience continued to grow. Williams and Di Virgilio's analytical lens mixed with their obvious love and passion for the team they covered endeared them to tens of thousands of Gator fans, which presented them with a unique opportunity a few seasons ago. At first, it started with a couple of comments here and there directed towards Di Virgilio about whether he thought "Gator Bait" could ever make a comeback. OPINION: SPORTS IS ONE OF AMERICA'S GREATEST TRADITIONS AND A POWERFUL FORCE THAT UNITES US "For two straight seasons, I basically polled our audience, which may or may not be representative of all of Gator Nation, to say 'does anybody really not want this?' Write to me," he explained. Di Virgilio said in two full seasons of pushing for responses, he only got one message that was against bringing it back against hundreds that were in favor. These messages, as he explained, came from a wide and diverse group of Gator fans, all of which cited very wholesome reasons for wanting the chant back in The Swamp. "It wasn't just young people, it wasn't just old people. It wasn't just people of a certain skin tone," Di Virgilio mentioned. "It felt like it was a very pure, wholesome reason for wanting it." Being a numbers guy, Di Virgilio had enough data to make his next move. The University of Florida hired Dr. Stuart Bell to be their new president in July of this year, and since the decision to reinstate "Gator Bait" was up to the head man himself, Di Virgilio saw his opportunity to act. "I had written to Dr. Bell a couple of weeks before we had everyone write to (him)," Di Virgilio said. "Here's my stance: I have limited information. You might have more information than I have. I would never want to do this if it was going to be divisive towards (other) Gators. I have no desire for that." "But if you do the research and you find that this is something a majority of Gator fans want... then on your own merits, maybe think about reinstituting it." With that, the die had been cast. Countless fans of the GNFP took Di Virgilio's call to action to heart and wrote impassioned pleas to the university president asking for their beloved chant back. They cited memories, tradition, and just the fact that it's a really catchy tune. But as the emails piled up in Dr. Bell's inbox and the season drew nearer, something must have finally swayed the new president. On the Friday before their first game against FAU, a clip was leaked of the Fightin' Gator Marching Band playing the familiar notes of "Gator Bait" on the practice field. Lo and behold, the following day, 90,000 rabid Florida fans led a full-throated rendition of the once-banned cheer. "Gator Bait" was back. Di Virgilio wants to be very clear: he doesn't want the credit for bringing the chant back to The Swamp. "I may have had 0.0001% to do with it," he explained. "Whether we were instrumental or not, someone else could have done it. I have no idea. We just felt like we wanted to push for something that brought back a lot of fond memories for us." Regardless, he and his podcast community can certainly say they at least had a hand in ushering back one of the best cheers in college football. "For me this is very apolitical," Di Virgilio said. "I think you want to do things that the majority of people want to do as long as it's not clearly violating any kind of legal or ethical boundary." As he explains, Di Virgilio recognizes that not everything will be universally loved, including the "Gator Bait" chant. Despite how popular the cheer's return has been on social media and in the Gator football community, some of the more vocal minority have bristled at the idea of "Gator Bait" making a comeback. "I hope that if you're on the side of, you don't love it, you understand that those that (do) want it, want it for very traditional Florida reasons," said Di Virgilio. articles.title: Trump’s Iran war now has a midterm election problem
articles.summary: Trump has tied the end of his war on Iran to the midterms. But with Iran holding firm, the political cost is mounting.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has claimed that the seven-month-long war with Iran will end “immediately after” the US midterm elections in ‌November, framing the ongoing conflict as an attempt by Tehran to influence the vote.

“They’re desperate to try and affect the election,” he told reporters on Wednesday.

Trump’s latest claims of Iranian capitulation are not new. Tehran has thus far withstood sustained strikes by the US and Israel intended to eradicate its military capacity, as well as a naval blockade of Iran’s ports intended to choke the country’s economy. In late August, the US ratcheted up the economic pressure even further, threatening secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners.

“It was a statement that was more likely meant for an internal [domestic] audience,” Ali Alavi, an Iran lecturer at SOAS University of London, said of Trump’s predictions of Iran’s post-election collapse. ”It was Trump’s method of communicating that the only reason it seemed as though he was failing in his Iran policy before the midterms is because Iran wanted it to be perceived that way.”

The cost of Iran’s failure to capitulate is being felt across the United States ahead of the midterms, which could see Trump’s Republican Party lose one or both houses of Congress.

Petrol prices – a key measure of the cost of living in the world’s largest economy – have climbed to a national average of $4.27 a gallon according to the American Automobile Association, up nearly 30 percent from a year ago.

Trump’s approval rating has also plunged from the high-40s when he returned to office in January 2025 to the low-to-mid 30s today.

The US electorate’s pain extends beyond the pump. A 2026 LendingTree survey found that 29 percent of buy-now-pay-later users had used the loans to buy groceries, while 47 percent said they had paid late on a buy-now-pay-later loan at least once in the past year.

Separately, economists at the University of Michigan have found that rising fuel costs and inflation linked to the war on Iran are weighing on consumer confidence and purchasing power.

“Iran has prepared for a long war,” Sanam Vakil, director of Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa programme, said. ”It may be that part of that was a secondary plan to hold out long enough to destabilise the US midterm elections once it realised that negotiations with the current administration were not going anywhere.”

Top Democrats, including the party’s Senate leader, Chuck Schumer, have been explicit in their calls for Trump to end the war on Iran.

Given Republican difficulties over the Iran war and other issues, Center for American Progress international policy analyst H.A. Hellyer described the situation ahead of the November 3 congressional midterms as one where the Democrats aren’t as much poised to win as the Republicans are positioned to lose.

“The question really is one of [voter] turnout,” he explained. “It’s not that many members of the Republican base will suddenly switch to supporting the Democrats, as much as they’ll stay home and not vote.”

Foreign policy, Hellyer said, rarely influenced voters, but “economics matter”.

“The price of things, like the petrol they get from the pump, matter – and it’s this that might swing [the election],” he added.

Irrespective of their claims of military success, both the US and Israel face a reckoning with an electorate that their leaders had promised easy victory: the US and Trump in November’s midterms and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu in a crucial general election in October. Iran, ruled by an unelected Supreme Leader and with no legislative elections scheduled until 2028, faces no such countdown.

“For Iran, victory is about surviving long enough to extract a serious diplomatic undertaking from its opponents that it won’t be attacked,” said Vakil of London-based Chatham House. “Victory is about demonstrating leverage, but negative leverage, in proving that it can still disrupt the world’s economy, no matter what the state of its military.”

“For some in the government, that includes retaining control over the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. “For others, that’s just a potential bargaining chip in negotiations, but for all: victory is survival and finding a way to convert it to stability. It’s a tall task.”
