articles.title: US Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed congressional map in Missouri
articles.summary: Rejection comes as Republican official in Missouri faces contempt charges for ignoring a lower court ruling.
articles.body:
The United States Supreme Court has again rejected a request from the administration of President Donald Trump to use electoral district maps that would favour his Republican party in the state of Missouri.

The court issued the latest order on Thursday, without noting any dissents to the decision, apparently clearing the way for Missouri to use the old map in mid-term elections this November that could determine which party controls the House of Representatives.

Earlier in the week, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Trump -appointee, rejected another request from the administration to put the new Republican-backed map into effect, without referring the case to the full nine-member court, or offering an explanation for his decision. Kavanaugh handles emergency matters from Missouri.

Contempt charges for Republican official

Missouri’s battle over its congressional districts has spanned more than a year and spawned confusion over which districts will be in place for voters.

The rejection on Thursday came hours after a federal judge allowed Missouri’s top court to proceed with a contempt hearing against Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins.

The state’s top court previously ordered Hoskins not to use a Trump-backed map in the general election and instead to use districts passed after the last census.

At the same time, US District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump -appointee, on Tuesday barred Hoskins from using anything other than the new map Trump supports.

The state Supreme Court then ordered Hoskins to appear for a contempt hearing on Thursday for not following its orders and instructing local election authorities to use the Trump-backed districts.

State attorneys representing Hoskins had asked Clark to halt the contempt hearing – but he declined.

Missouri was the second Republican-led state, after Texas, to enact new districts after Trump urged Republicans last year to redraw House districts to their advantage ahead of the midterm elections.

The revised Missouri districts target a Kansas City-based seat held by Democratic Representative Emanuel Cleaver by shedding parts into neighbouring districts and stretching the remainder into rural Republican areas. The goal is to help Republicans win seven of the state’s eight House seats in the midterm elections — a gain of one seat.

Redistricting opponents collected hundreds of thousands of petition signatures seeking to force a statewide vote on the new districts. They submitted the signatures in December. But Hoskins waited until August — on the same day as Missouri’s primary — to reject the petition. Hoskins asserted that a referendum petition could not be used for congressional redistricting.

The delay allowed Missouri to use the new districts in its August primary. Republican state officials have argued it would violate voters’ federal rights to switch districts before the general election.

But the Missouri Supreme Court last week ordered Hoskins to put the redistricting referendum on the November ballot, which he did. It also ruled that the new districts never became law and instead were suspended retroactively to the December petition submission.

The state then appealed to the US Supreme Court to block the state court’s findings. Justice Brett Kavanaugh rejected their request.

The court barred Hoskins from using the new map and said the old map — passed by Republican legislators in 2022 after the last census — must be used in the November election. The US Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to hear an appeal of that decision. But Clark issued his conflicting order moments later.

articles.title: Florida attorney general sues Netflix over ‘bait-and-switch’ on privacy for kids
articles.summary: Florida’s attorney general filed a sweeping lawsuit against Netflix, accusing the streaming giant of misleading consumers about its data collection practices.
articles.body: Florida’s attorney general filed a sweeping lawsuit Wednesday against Netflix, accusing the Hollywood streaming giant of misleading consumers about its data collection practices and exposing kids to “addictive” design features. “Netflix told Florida families they could pay a monthly fee to escape Big Tech surveillance. That was false,” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said in a statement accompanying the filing. “Netflix collected detailed data on children and families, designed its product to keep kids watching, and then commercialized that information to launch the advertising business it promised never to build,” Uthmeier added in part. In response to a request for comment Thursday, a Netflix spokesperson said the company “takes our members’ privacy seriously.” “We comply with privacy and data‑protection laws everywhere we operate and have dedicated safeguards in place for kids who watch content on Netflix,” the spokesperson added. “This lawsuit lacks merit and we intend to vigorously defend the matter in court.” Uthmeier’s suit opens another front in Florida’s legal crusade against major technology platforms. Uthmeier’s office filed suit against OpenAI in early June, accusing the artificial intelligence company of putting profit over safety. The same month, the state sued TikTok, claiming the social media application violated state child safety law. In the 66-page suit against Netflix, Florida alleges it orchestrated a “years-long bait-and-switch.” Uthmeier’s office claims Netflix spent years marketing its subscription service as an ad-free alternative to the data-driven business models of Silicon Valley behemoths like Google and Facebook, all while assuring parents that the platform’s kids profiles were “safe.” However, according to the Florida plaintiffs, Netflix was designing systems to collect information about how users interacted with the platform, including what they watched, clicked, paused, replayed and skipped. The state alleges Netflix used the “addictive” autoplay feature to keep adult and child users watching while logging “billions” of behavioral data points. The streaming service introduced an ad-supported plan in November 2022 as part of a wider push to drive revenue amid slowing subscriber growth. The platform currently offers two ad-free plans, Standard and Premium, as well as a lower-priced Standard with ads plan. “Netflix’s years-long bait-and-switch has led the company right to where it promised never to be: addicting children and families to its platform, mining those users for data, and then converting that data into lucrative intelligence for global advertising juggernauts,” Florida says in the complaint. “This is deceptive conduct that violates Florida law.” Netflix shares a privacy statement and terms of use with members annually, according to the platform. The documents provide explanations of the company’s advertising and privacy practices, as well as members’ rights and controls. Netflix subscribers can manage their advertising preferences and turn off behavioral ads at any time, according to the service. The service also offers parental controls that allow parents to filter content by maturity rating or block specific programming. Members can disable autoplay for episodes and trailers at any time, while parents have control over autoplay features on kids’ profiles, according to Netflix. Florida’s suit comes four months after Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed his own complaint against Netflix, accusing the platform of “spying on” people in his state, including children, and collecting user data without consent. “Netflix is not the ad-free and kid-friendly platform it claims to be. Instead, it has misled consumers while exploiting their private data to make billions,” said Paxton, also the state’s Republican nominee for U.S. Senate. In a statement at the time, a Netflix spokesperson said the lawsuit “lacks merit and is based on inaccurate and distorted information.” Florida is demanding a jury trial on its allegation that Netflix is violating the state’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act and the state’s Digital Bill of Rights. It is seeking a court ruling that would, among other things, order Netflix to “purge all data deceptively collected from Floridians.” Uthmeier, a Republican who took office in February 2025, previously served as chief of staff to Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. DeSantis appointed Uthmeier to replace former state attorney general Ashley Moody, who resigned as attorney general to fill the U.S. Senate seat vacated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

articles.title: A Los Angeles artist disappeared into a Puerto Rican forest and spent 40 years building a bizarre underground home from discarded materials
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A Los Angeles artist spent about four decades creating a unique underground home in the forests of Puerto Rico, turning discarded materials into a maz.
articles.body: A Los Angeles artist spent about four decades creating a unique underground home in the forests of Puerto Rico, turning discarded materials into a maze of tunnels, chambers and artworks. Known as Termitopia, the structure sits on a mountain near Las Marías and was built by Brian Birdsall, who moved away from Los Angeles and made a life in the Puerto Rican countryside. Rather than following conventional building methods, he shaped the home around the idea of reusing materials that would otherwise become waste. The result is part home, part artwork and part underground world.Los Angeles artist built a home from discarded materials in Puerto Rican forestAccording to Atlas Obscura, Termitopia was the brainchild of Birdsall, described as an artist refugee from Los Angeles who spent around 40 years in the Puerto Rican forest developing the free-form structure. The home was made from discarded fishnet and a type of cement that Birdsall developed himself.The construction was unusual from the beginning. Instead of creating a conventional house with clearly separated rooms, Birdsall carved a network of passages and chambers into the mountainside. Atlas Obscura reports that the arrangement can be compared to a human-sized rabbit warren, with tunnels cutting through the underground space.The approach also reflected Birdsall's interest in making use of materials that other people might throw away. According to Atlas Obscura, Termitopia followed a termitic principle, in which construction relies on reusable materials rather than generating large quantities of waste.The idea gave the project a character that was very different from an ordinary home. Its walls, tunnels and objects were shaped around whatever could be reused, allowing the building to grow into something more like a personal landscape than a standard residence.A home shaped around reuse and inventionAccording to Instructables, he is a Los Angeles refugee living in the backwoods of Puerto Rico and says he built his own home from discarded nylon fishnet and cement. It also reports that he created and shared numerous practical projects using readily available or leftover materials.His work reflects a hands-on approach in which everyday objects and discarded materials could be turned into something useful or unexpected. The connection between those projects and Termitopia is especially revealing. The underground home was not simply a building assembled from a fixed set of conventional materials. It was part of a wider creative habit of experimenting, adapting and finding new uses for things that might otherwise be discarded.What made the Termitopia so uniqueTermitopia was also designed as an artistic environment. Atlas Obscura describes the interiors as falling somewhere between the organic forms associated with Antoni Gaudí and the underground settlements of Cappadocia.Its spaces included more than bare tunnels. The complex contained artworks and objects, including musical PVC piping and cartoon-like face sculptures. Decorative details were incorporated into the concrete structure, giving the underground passages a playful and sometimes surreal quality.Birdsall also worked with other artists. Atlas Obscura reports Pablo Verona and Daniel Polnau as frequent collaborators. Both were part of Puerto Rico's art scene, and together the artists used what they regarded as an abundant resource(discarded material), to develop their creative surroundings.This meant that Termitopia was never simply about shelter. The building itself became an evolving piece of artwork, with its spaces and found-material creations forming part of the experience.The forest became part of the experience in the houseThe location added another dimension to the project. Termitopia was built in the western Puerto Rican countryside near Las Marías, surrounded by forest rather than by the crowded streets of a city.At the top of the structure was a roof deck overlooking the surrounding jungle. Although much of the complex was enclosed underground, parts of it were exposed to the outside environment, linking the interior with the landscape around it.Atlas Obscura reports that the site was roughly a two-hour drive from San Juan. It also records that the structure had stairs and some exposure to the elements, making practical footwear more suitable for exploring it.The setting helped make the building feel separate from ordinary urban life. Its tunnels disappeared into the mountain while the roof deck opened towards the forest, creating a sharp contrast between the enclosed underground rooms and the landscape outside.Termitopia became a record of a very different way of buildingOver roughly 40 years, Birdsall's project developed into a sprawling combination of home, artwork and experiment. Its importance was not simply in its appearance, but in the way it challenged familiar ideas about what a house should be made from and how it should take shape.The project also demonstrated how discarded materials could become part of a creative process rather than ending up as waste. Termitopia is now permanently closed, according to Atlas Obscura. Yet the story of the underground home remains fascinating that an artist left Los Angeles, settled in the Puerto Rican forest and spent decades turning discarded materials into a private world beneath the trees.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Israel arrests 100 Palestinians in a week as West Bank pogroms continue
articles.summary: Palestinian Prisoner’s Society says detained include children, journalists and ex-prisoner freed in recent exchange deal
articles.body:
Israeli forces have detained more than 100 Palestinians in the West Bank over the past week, including children, the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society (PPS) says, as pogroms continue across the occupied territory.

The Palestinian rights group, which tracks detentions and conditions in Israeli custody, said in a statement on Thursday that Israeli forces have intensified detention operations across the territory, alleging a range of abuses including field interrogations, physical assaults, threats against detainees’ families and, in some cases, extrajudicial killings.

The group said that Israeli forces conducted extensive home raids during the operations, searching and damaging properties and, in some cases, occupying homes for military use.

It added that Palestinians were sometimes held to pressure relatives, and that entire neighbourhoods were swept during raids. Children were also arrested, it said.

Among those detained over the past week was Ahmad al-Sayfi, a former prisoner from Birzeit who had been released under a recent prisoner exchange deal, the PPS said.

Journalists Muath Amarneh and Sabri Jibril were also among those detained, along with several other former prisoners.

The PPS also said Israeli settlers carried out attacks on Palestinians and their property , including assaults, road blockades and attacks on vehicles, which it said took place with the protection of Israeli forces.

The group said Israeli forces have detained more than 25,000 Palestinians in the West Bank, and thousands more in Gaza, since Israel’s genocidal war began in October 2023.

In a dawn raid on Thursday, Israeli forces arrested 15 Palestinians in the town of Burqa, in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

Wafa said soldiers stormed the town for six hours, raiding homes and arresting their owners before withdrawing.

Burqa, which lies northwest of Nablus city, has been subjected to frequent attacks by settlers and soldiers in recent weeks, as well as numerous home demolitions .

Israeli forces also detained Salloum Radwan, a young man from the town of Azzun, east of Qalqilya, for several hours and seized his truck, Wafa reported.

Al Jazeera correspondent Givara Budeiri, reporting from Ramallah, said Israeli special forces also raided the town of Beitunia, near central Ramallah, on Thursday, entering an apartment and arresting two Palestinian men.

“They caused damage and destruction inside the home,” Budeiri said. “The two men were transferred to an Israeli prison, and the special force subsequently withdrew.”

Budeiri said Israeli forces also demolished a house in Battir, west of Bethlehem.

The Israeli military said in a statement it had arrested at least 20 Palestinians in the Arroub refugee camp, south of Bethlehem, alleging they had been planning attacks.

Budeiri also reported that settlers stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem on Thursday morning and performed religious rituals there, part of what she described as a now daily occurrence.

The Jerusalem Governorate warned that Israeli settlers could exploit upcoming Jewish holidays to shift from a longstanding time-based division of the site towards a spatial one, effectively partitioning the compound.

The Palestinian presidency and Foreign Ministry issued similar warnings, stressing that the entire site is an Islamic holy place.

Israeli police said they had deployed additional forces across occupied Jerusalem and the West Bank ahead of the holidays.

articles.title: The Trump-to-Mamdani voter is real. How does the trend affect the midterms?
articles.summary: Exit polls suggest 9 percent of Trump voters backed New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, despite ideological differences.
articles.body:
New York City, United States – Ron Barba, 56, voted for New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani last year. He also voted for United States President Donald Trump the year before.

One is a democratic socialist. The other is a deep-red Republican. Barba, a tall, outgoing man with bright eyes and a chin dotted with white stubble, knows the two politicians hail from opposite ends of the political spectrum. He does not care.

“Both of them were awesome,” Barba said.

Barba has become the face of a small but striking trend in New York City. Exit polling after last year's mayoral race suggested that 9 percent of the city's Trump voters in 2024 proceeded to back Mamdani.

Such swing voters could be critical in the upcoming midterm elections on November 3. Control over Congress is likely to be decided by a few key toss-up races.

But experts caution against reading the Trump-Mamdani crossover as a new voting bloc.

Rather, they say it's part of a familiar trend of voters seeking relief among populists for their economic frustrations, as well as searching for a break from the political establishment.

“A lot of times those people are reacting to economic performance, essentially,” said Brian Shaffner, a political science professor at Tufts University.

“And a lot of the time, they are just voting against whoever's in office or voting for the outsider candidate who they think will shake things up.”

articles.title: New technology may bring more 9/11 victims' families closure
articles.summary: Since the attacks, New York officials are working with new, complex technology to find traces of more than 1,000 victims.
articles.body:
For 25 years, the only physical trace Juliette Scauso has had from the last day of her father's life was his mangled firefighter helmet.

Scauso's father, Dennis - part of a New York City Fire Department (FDNY) hazmat unit for 12 years - initially was not scheduled to work on 11 September, 2001, but switched shifts for the overtime pay.

The Long Island father of four was likely in the South Tower of the World Trade Center when it collapsed, the Scauso family was told. The helmet with his badge number was found months later.

"I've spent essentially my entire life knowing my father died, and learning to live with the fact that we never recovered him," said Scauso, who was four when he died.

Dennis Scauso is one of more than 1,000 people killed on September 11 in New York who have yet to be identified, according to New York City's Office of Chief Medical Examiner. Nearly 3,000 people died in the World Trade Center attacks that day.

Last month, the city announced the identity of a previously unknown victim of the terrorist attacks - the 1,654th person - using a new technology called forensic investigative genetic genealogy - or FIGG.

"There is real promise in using this approach," said Angela Soler, director of forensic anthropology in the city's medical examiner office. "There's hope for more families to receive answers, and hopefully we'll be able to test more remains in the future using this technology as well."

Since 9/11, Soler's office has sought to identify the remains of the 2,753 victims who died in the World Trade Center. So far, 60 percent of those killed have been identified.

"It's been one of the most complex identification efforts that I think anybody has ever really experienced," Soler said.

25 years later, DNA matches are still being made

Efforts to identify victims have been complicated by a number of factors.

Human remains were damaged in the plane crashes and fires caused by jet fuel, meaning the office had only portions of victims for DNA samples, Soler said.

Scauso added that because of the timing of the attacks, many firefighters were changing shifts, but some stayed to help, grabbing whatever extra gear they could find. This meant some first responders recovered were wearing uniforms with others' names, complicating identification.

The World Trade Center site also had many more victims than the other 9/11 terrorist attack sites.

The remains of five of the 184 people killed when American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the Pentagon were never identified because of similar conditions. According to the National Park Service, enough remains were recovered to use DNA, dental records and fingerprints to identify all 40 victims aboard United Airlines flight 93, which crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

Remains from the World Trade Center have been packaged and sealed to help preserve DNA for testing in the years to come. Soon after the attacks, individuals were identified using fingerprints or dental records, but as time went on, when neither was available, the office turned to DNA. Officials were able to use new technology to extract DNA and retest the same remains.

"That's why all these years down the road, we're still getting new identifications, because we're just continuing to retest and retry with every new technology that becomes available," Soler said.

DNA technology has helped the office identify 1,495 victims since 9/11 - some solely with DNA and others with multiple methods - according to the medical examiner's office.

Last year, the city announced that with the help of DNA, 24 years later, it had identified three new victims - Ryan Fitzgerald, a 26-year-old currency trader, Babara Keating, a 72-year-old who was aboard American Airlines Flight 11 from Boston to Los Angeles, and a woman whose family kept her identity private.

Soler said the new FIGG technology uses whole genome sequencing - which provides a way to read someone's entire genetic code. It means investigators can make more potential matches to family members who are more distant relatives of the victim. Once those matches are made, the New York Police Department helps find relatives who are closer to the victims.

The medical examiner's office in New York still gets weekly calls from loved ones asking about someone whose remains were never recovered.

Many have never been able to bury a loved one, but some families choose to leave the remains - once found - at a repository at the 9/11 memorial site in New York. The repository was built into the bedrock of the World Trade Center site and can only be accessed by medical examiner staff. A nearby private space, known as the reflection room, is available for families to mourn.

"That's where their loved one was in their last moments, and that's where they want them to stay", Soler said.

Some don't want to be notified, perhaps because the confirmation is too painful, said Soler, who helps inform families.

Scauso is one of those people. She knows people who, in recent years, got a call that a relative finally has been identified. The thought of being next on the list is scary for her family, who has worked hard to keep the memory of her father - a jack of all trades and a lover of jazz - alive.

"At this point, an identification wouldn't change the reality of his death. It wouldn't give me back my father, and I don't necessarily want to reopen something that has become part of the way I've learned to live and grieve," she said. "Especially 25 years later, it's going to open up the wounds again."

But, Scauso said, the technology is important.

Soler has seen the news provide a mix of both relief and sadness. "It's confirmation of something that they always knew to be true - they knew their loved one died on 9/11, but I think for many families, there's still that question in the back of their mind until the remains are formally identified," Soler said.

"Maybe they're reliving it a little bit more now, having this new identification. But at the same time, it closes one chapter of their journey after 9/11," she added.

To Soler - and some of her current colleagues who also were on the ground during 9/11 - the work is deeply personal. Workers from their office arrived at Ground Zero after the planes hit the towers, and were there when the buildings collapsed.

They are aware it is unlikely they will identify every victim of the New York attacks. In some instances, there may be no remains of a victim at all. Still, they have no plans to stop.

"As long as there's families looking for answers, we'll continue searching for them," she said.

articles.body: Aaron Rodgers is going out with a bang. Entering what he calls his final season in the NFL, the Pittsburgh Steelers QB took aim at former girlfriend, Danica Patrick, this week in a sit-down with teammate Cam Heyward. "I dated Danica. She had just retired. She was depressed and not fun to be around. But I didn’t leave her because I was trying to be there and be a good partner. Then it was going a certain direction obviously. "She tells a story that she was so blindsided and getting left by you, and that he leaves a trail of blood around him. And I’m like, what are you talking about? That’s not what happened." Danica Patrick once had a very different story . Lord have mercy. Danica Patrick and Aaron Rodgers haven't dated for years, and it's still the most toxic relationship of all time. She called the future Hall of Famer "emotionally abusive," and accused him of leaving a "trail of blood" toward the end of their relationship. articles.title: Hydrofoil could provide link to Isles of Scilly, says firm
articles.summary: A marine technology company is running demonstrations of a hydrofoil which could run in winter.
articles.body:
A marine technology firm has been showcasing an all-weather electric hydrofoil vessel it says could travel between Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly.

Artemis Technologies said the hydrofoil, which uses underwater wings to lift the boat out of the water, could operate in winter when seas are choppy.

John Patterson, from the firm, said said four days of demonstrations in Newlyn and St Mary's were "really exciting" for the region.

They follow a feasibility study run with the Council of the Isles of Scilly to see if the technology "could help make life easier for the locals" with "quick, clean, efficient transit".

If it gets the go-ahead Patterson said a full-size ferry could take 150 passengers at a speed of 32 knots between Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly in just over an hour.

"The whole joy of the hydrofoil system is it lifts the vessel out," he said, adding it made for a "more comfortable ride".

The feasibility study run with the council and transport firm Connected Places Catapult was aimed at showing "modern technology can provide an alternate solution which may be able to overcome the issues which the Isles of Scilly have in the depths of winter", he added.

Patterson said the firm was looking for an operator and the earliest it could arrive at the islands was "probably 18 months to two years, with fair winds behind us".

"This is all about showing that [with] modern technology there is a solution which can be adopted for cheap, fast transfer between the mainland and the Scilly Isles," he said.

Robert Francis, lead member for transport, economy of tourism at the Council of the Isles of Scilly said: "We are backing the project because we believe it may well be a really good opportunity for us.

"Our community is struggling with unaffordable passenger fares and unaffordable freight costs and this really green 100% electric vessel is going to be the future we believe."

He said it would be "huge" if the boat could run through the winter as "we've got families marooned on the islands".

"We're hoping this is going to operate all year round and it's going to give us some affordable travel because connectivity is everything for us," he said.
